# A. What forecasting is for {.sdaia-dark background-gradient="linear-gradient(135deg, #1C355E, #00C9A7)"}

Ch 1 · Why forecast at all

## Forecasts exist to change decisions

::: {.reveal-shown}
- **Inventory**: how much stock to hold
- **Staffing**: how many people to roster
- **Energy**: when generation must ramp up
- **Finance**: cash flow and budget targets
:::


::: {.cardbox .teal}
A forecast is only useful if it **changes a decision**.
:::

::: {.notes}
The decision dictates the entire setup: the forecast horizon, the time frequency, and the error metric you care about.
:::

## Three factors dictate predictability

::: {.reveal-shown}
1. **Understanding**: how well we understand the drivers
2. **Data**: how much historical data exists
3. **Influence**: whether the forecast changes the outcome
:::


::: {.notes}
Point 3 is key: if a demand forecast causes price cuts or stockouts, it alters future demand (self-fulfilling or self-defeating forecasts).
:::

## High data and clear drivers make series predictable

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.cardbox .teal}
[Electricity Demand]{.card-title}

- Clear physical drivers (weather, calendar)
- High volume of historical data
- Forecast does not change demand
- $\rightarrow$ **Highly predictable**
:::
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.cardbox}
[Exchange Rates]{.card-title}

- Weakly understood drivers
- Forecast moves the market
- No stable recurring pattern
- $\rightarrow$ **Hard to beat today's price**
:::
:::
::::

## Pure time series models require no future drivers {.smaller}

Forecasting hourly **electricity demand (ED)**, three ways to write the same job:

::: {.cardbox .teal}
[1. Explanatory]{.card-title} — *why is demand what it is?* Every driver on the
right needs its own forecast first.

$$\small \text{ED} = f(\text{temperature},\ \text{economy},\ \text{population},\ \text{time of day},\ \text{day of week},\ \text{error})$$
:::

::: {.cardbox .navy}
[2. Time series]{.card-title} — *what happened next last time?* Everything on the
right is already recorded.

$$\small \text{ED}_{t+1} = f(\text{ED}_t,\ \text{ED}_{t-1},\ \text{ED}_{t-2},\ \text{ED}_{t-3},\ \ldots,\ \text{error})$$
:::

::: {.cardbox .purple}
[3. Mixed]{.card-title} — *dynamic regression:* past demand **plus** drivers, so
the drivers' forecast error rides along.

$$\small \text{ED}_{t+1} = f(\text{ED}_t,\ \text{temperature}_{t+1},\ \text{time of day},\ \text{day of week},\ \text{error})$$
:::

**Course focus:** Days 1–2 stay on **model 2**. Day 3 goes further.

::: {.notes}
This is fpppy 1.4. The point is not that explanatory models are worse — it is that
their right-hand side is unavailable at forecast time, so you end up forecasting
the predictors too, and inherit that error.
:::

## Past history avoids missing future predictors

Time series models only need to know: **what happened next last time?**

::: {.reveal-shown}
- External drivers may not be available
- Future driver values are often unknown (e.g. future gas prices)
- The real system is often too complex to specify
:::

::: {.notes}
Relying on past history is not laziness; it is often the most dependable, honest model choice in production.
:::

# B. What is in a time series {.sdaia-dark background-gradient="linear-gradient(135deg, #1C355E, #FF7A5C)"}

Ch 2 · Patterns and components

## Trend, seasonality, and cycles are distinct patterns

::: {.reveal-shown}
- **Trend**: Long-term increase or decrease
- **Seasonality**: Repeating pattern at a **fixed, known period** (day, week, year)
- **Cycle**: Rises and falls with **no fixed period** (business cycles)
:::

::: {.notes}
Trend does not have to be linear. Cycles are usually longer than seasonality and vary in length.
:::

## Seasonality has a fixed calendar period; cycles vary

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.cardbox .teal}
[Seasonality]{.card-title}

- **Known, fixed period**
- Driven by the calendar / clock
- Can be counted on reliably
:::
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.cardbox}
[Cycle]{.card-title}

- **Variable, unknown period**
- Driven by economic / natural factors
- Turning points are hard to predict
:::
:::
::::


::: {.callout-important}
## Common Mistake
Treating a cycle as seasonality causes models to predict peaks at the wrong time with false confidence.
:::

## Four series show four distinct temporal patterns

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Plot
```{python}
#| fig-width: 10
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(10, 4.5))

P.plot_series(spine, ax=axes[0, 0], title="Trend + seasonality (retail)",
              ylabel="turnover ($M)")
P.plot_series(beer, ax=axes[0, 1], title="Seasonality + drifting trend (beer)",
              color=P.BLUE, ylabel="megalitres")
P.plot_series(lynx, ax=axes[1, 0], title="Cycle, no fixed period (lynx)",
              color=P.PINK, ylabel="pelts traded")
P.plot_series(noise, ax=axes[1, 1], title="No pattern (white noise)",
              color=P.GREY, ylabel="z")
P.thin_xticks(axes, n=4)
# lynx is annual and the question is how many years apart the peaks fall,
# so that panel gets a decade label and a tick on every single year.
P.year_xticks(axes[1, 0], step=10, minor=1)
for ax in axes.ravel():
    ax.set_xlabel("")
plt.show()
```

### Code
```python
# Datasets:
# 1. Victorian retail takeaway turnover: spine = D.spine()
# 2. Australian quarterly beer production: beer = D.beer()
# 3. Canadian lynx pelts (annual): lynx = D.lynx()
# 4. Simulated white noise: noise = D.white_noise(n=len(spine), seed=7)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(10, 5.4))
P.plot_series(spine, ax=axes[0, 0], title="Trend + seasonality (retail)", ylabel="turnover ($M)")
P.plot_series(beer, ax=axes[0, 1], title="Seasonality + drifting trend (beer)", color=P.BLUE, ylabel="megalitres")
P.plot_series(lynx, ax=axes[1, 0], title="Cycle, no fixed period (lynx)", color=P.PINK, ylabel="pelts traded")
P.plot_series(noise, ax=axes[1, 1], title="No pattern (white noise)", color=P.GREY, ylabel="z")

# Decade labels, plus a tick on every year, so the peak-to-peak gaps are countable
P.year_xticks(axes[1, 0], step=10, minor=1)
```

:::

::: {.notes}
The lynx peaks occur 8–11 years apart, never the exact same gap. This is a cycle, not seasonality.
:::

## Time series split into trend, season, and remainder

::: {.reveal-shown}
- **Additive**: $y_t = S_t + T_t + R_t$
- **Multiplicative**: $y_t = S_t \times T_t \times R_t$
:::


| Component | Meaning |
|---|---|
| $S_t$ | **Seasonal** component (repeating calendar pattern) |
| $T_t$ | **Trend-Cycle** component (underlying direction) |
| $R_t$ | **Remainder** (random noise / unexplained variation) |

Decomposition cannot separate trend from cycle, so $T_t$ carries both. That is
why it is written trend-cycle.

## Expanding swings require multiplicative models

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Plot
```{python}
#| fig-width: 9.5
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9.5, 3.1))
P.plot_series(beer.tail(120), ax=axes[0], color=P.BLUE, ylabel="megalitres",
              title="Additive: swing size is constant")
P.plot_series(souvenirs, ax=axes[1], color=P.ORANGE, ylabel="sales ($)",
              title="Multiplicative: swing grows with level")
P.thin_xticks(axes, n=4)
for ax in axes:
    ax.set_xlabel("")
plt.show()
```

### Code
```python
# Datasets:
# 1. Australian beer production (last 10 years / 120 obs): beer.tail(120)
# 2. Souvenir shop sales: souvenirs = D.souvenirs()

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9.5, 3.1))
P.plot_series(beer.tail(120), ax=axes[0], color=P.BLUE, ylabel="megalitres",
              title="Additive: swing size is constant")
P.plot_series(souvenirs, ax=axes[1], color=P.ORANGE, ylabel="sales ($)",
              title="Multiplicative: swing grows with level")
```

:::

::: {.cardbox .purple}
- Constant swing $\rightarrow$ **Additive**
- Growing swing $\rightarrow$ **Multiplicative** (fix with log transform)
:::


::: {.notes}
Point at the right panel and ask what a model fitted to the 1988 swing would predict
for 1993. Far too small. A log transform turns that growing swing into a constant
one, which is the fix used all through segment 4.
:::

## The Golden Rule {.sdaia-dark background-gradient="linear-gradient(135deg, #1C355E, #625D9C)"}

::: {.r-fit-text}
The order **is** the data.
:::


::: {.reveal-shown}
- Never shuffle time series data
- Never use random train/test splits
- Never use standard k-fold cross-validation
:::

::: {.notes}
Random shuffling allows models to look into the future. Day 2 introduces rolling-origin evaluation.
:::

## Same values, shuffled: every pattern is gone

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Plot
```{python}
#| fig-width: 10
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
y = spine["y"].to_numpy()
shuffled = rng.permutation(y)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 3.4), sharey=True)
P.plot_series(spine, ax=axes[0], color=P.BLACK, ylabel="turnover ($M)",
              title="Original: trend and season")
P.plot_series(spine.assign(y=shuffled), ax=axes[1], color=P.ORANGE,
              title="Shuffled: same 441 values, new order")
P.thin_xticks(axes, n=4)
for ax in axes:
    ax.set_xlabel("")
plt.show()
```

### Code
```python
# Dataset: spine = D.spine() (441 monthly observations)
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
y = spine["y"].to_numpy()
shuffled = rng.permutation(y)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 3.4), sharey=True)
P.plot_series(spine, ax=axes[0], color=P.BLACK, ylabel="turnover ($M)",
              title="Original: trend and season")
P.plot_series(spine.assign(y=shuffled), ax=axes[1], color=P.ORANGE,
              title="Shuffled: same 441 values, new order")
```

:::

::: {.reveal-shown}
- Same mean, same variance, same histogram
- Nothing left to forecast from: the order was the only structure
:::

::: {.notes}
Ask the room what a model could possibly learn from the right-hand panel. Nothing, and
yet its summary statistics are identical to the left. Day 2 measures this properly.
:::

# C. Seeing the patterns {.sdaia-dark background-gradient="linear-gradient(135deg, #1C355E, #9B8EC0)"}

Ch 2.2–2.5 · The four plots

## Four plots, four questions

| Plot | Core Question |
|---|---|
| **Time plot** | What does the overall series look like? |
| **Seasonal plot** | What is the repeating annual shape? |
| **Subseries plot** | How does each specific month/quarter evolve? |
| **Lag plot** | Is $y_t$ related to $y_{t-k}$? (next deck) |


::: {.callout-tip}
## Start with the Time Plot
Always check the time plot first for outliers, gaps, and structural breaks.
:::

## Time plots reveal long-term trend and variance growth

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Plot
```{python}
#| fig-width: 9.5
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9.5, 3.0))
P.plot_series(spine, ax=ax, ylabel="turnover ($M)",
              title=f"{D.SPINE_ID}, monthly")
P.thin_xticks(ax, n=6)
plt.show()
```

### Code
```python
# Data: Victorian takeaway food turnover (D.spine())
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9.5, 3.0))
P.plot_series(spine, ax=ax, ylabel="turnover ($M)",
              title=f"{D.SPINE_ID}, monthly")
```

:::

::: {.reveal-shown}
- Upward trend, roughly sixfold over 37 years
- The seasonal swing widens as the level rises
- Sharp 2009 step and 2000 dip: investigate breaks before modelling
:::


::: {.notes}
Spend a moment here. This is the series the whole course runs on, so the room should

:::

## Seasonal plots expose repeating annual shapes

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Plot
```{python}
#| fig-width: 10
sp = D.add_calendar(spine)
recent = sp[sp["year"] >= sp["year"].max() - 9]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9.5, 3.7))
P.seasonal_plot(recent, "year", "month", ax=ax, season_labels=P.MONTH_LABELS,
                ylabel="turnover ($M)", xlabel="", colorbar=True,
                title="One line per year, last 10 years")
plt.show()
```

### Code
```python
# Dataset: Victorian retail takeaway turnover (last 10 years):
# spine = D.spine(); sp = D.add_calendar(spine)
recent = sp[sp["year"] >= sp["year"].max() - 9]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9.5, 3.7))
P.seasonal_plot(recent, "year", "month", ax=ax, season_labels=P.MONTH_LABELS,
                ylabel="turnover ($M)", xlabel="", colorbar=True,
                title="One line per year, last 10 years")
```

:::

::: {.reveal-shown}
- Every year peaks in **December** and troughs in **February**
- The shape repeats while the level climbs: that is seasonality, not cycle
:::

::: {.notes}
Ten years, not all 37. Over the full span the level grows sixfold, so the lines stack by year and the shape is unreadable.
:::

## Subseries plots isolate pure seasonal means

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Plot
```{python}
#| fig-width: 10
fig, axes = P.subseries_plot(D.add_calendar(beer), "quarter",
                             ylabel="megalitres", season_labels=P.QUARTER_LABELS,
                             title="Beer production by quarter, 1956 to 2010 (orange line = quarter mean)")
plt.show()
```

### Code
```python
# Dataset: Australian quarterly beer production (1956 to 2010): beer = D.beer()
fig, axes = P.subseries_plot(D.add_calendar(beer), "quarter",
                             ylabel="megalitres", season_labels=P.QUARTER_LABELS,
                             title="Beer production by quarter, 1956 to 2010 (orange line = quarter mean)")
```

:::

::: {.cardbox .teal}
Differences in the horizontal means highlight the pure seasonal pattern.
:::

## Strong trend obscures raw month-to-month means

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Plot
```{python}
#| fig-width: 10
fig, axes = P.subseries_plot(sp, "month", ylabel="turnover ($M)",
                             season_labels=P.MONTH_LABELS,
                             title="Spine turnover by month, 1982 to 2018")
plt.show()
```

### Code
```python
# Dataset: Victorian retail takeaway turnover (D.spine(), 1982-2018):
# sp = D.add_calendar(spine)
fig, axes = P.subseries_plot(sp, "month", ylabel="turnover ($M)",
                             season_labels=P.MONTH_LABELS,
                             title="Spine turnover by month, 1982 to 2018")
```

:::

::: {.callout-important}
## Trend Obscures Month-to-Month Means
When trend growth is this large (6x), seasonal differences appear tiny until trend is removed with **decomposition** (next deck).
:::

::: {.notes}
Ask the room which month is highest here. Nobody can tell. Then flip back two
slides to the seasonal plot, where December is obvious. Same data, different
subtraction.
:::

## Verify timestamp continuity before fitting models

```{python}
#| echo: true
gaps = spine["ds"].diff().dt.days
print("Inferred frequency :", pd.infer_freq(spine["ds"]))
print("Duplicate stamps   :", spine["ds"].duplicated().sum())
print("Gaps > 1 month     :", int((gaps > 32).sum()))
```


::: {.callout-important}
## Silent Gaps Break Models
A missing row shifts every seasonal lag that follows. Always check frequency before modelling.
:::

::: {.notes}
Run this on every series before anything else. A missing month does not raise, it
silently renumbers every seasonal lag after it, and you find out much later when a
seasonal model quietly stops working. Exercise 1.2 has students break it on purpose.
:::
